extracted.intended_audience: small law firms and SMMEs in South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Practical legal and procedural standards for obtaining and maintaining registered designs and patents in South Africa, plus related copyright/performers' rights guidance. Covers statutory requirements, filing steps, timelines, ownership, exclusions, renewal and enforcement considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of subsistence of copyright and ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: As there is no certificate of registration for copyright works, you need to prove the subsistence of copyright and the rights of ownership of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep proper records surrounding the creation, updating or acquisition of any copyright work. Registration of a cinematograph film serves to alleviate the burden of proof of rights. When commissioning work, enter into a written agreement assigning the copyright; check employment contracts to identify scope and capacity of creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration depends on the type of work: literary, artistic, and musical works are protected for the lifetime of the author plus 50 years from the end of the year in which the author dies; other works, 50 years after the work is made available to the public, published, or made; State works, 50 years from the end of the year the work was first published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Berne Convention 50 years is a minimum; some jurisdictions (US, EU) have 70 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic rights under copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright grants the owner the exclusive right to do or authorise others to perform restricted acts, primarily relating to reproduction or adaptation of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Copyright Act details a list of restricted acts per category of work; these generally relate to copying or commercial exploitation. Unauthorized use of the substantial part (quality not quantity) without consent infringes copyright and may be an offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral rights under copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: The author retains rights of paternity (the right to claim authorship) and integrity (to object to distortion, mutilation, or modification prejudicial to reputation), even when the author does not own the copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral rights persist independently of economic ownership and can be enforced where reputation is prejudiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of copyright (formal requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright is movable property and must be assigned in writing, licensed, transmitted by will/testament, or by operation of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignment must be in writing and signed on behalf of the assignor, and the work being assigned must be clearly identified in the assignment agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neighbouring rights / performers' protection rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers' protection rights are governed by copyright laws and the Performers’ Protection Act 11 of 1967; the Act regulates rights of performers, producers and broadcasters and offers protection for performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments introduced performing rights for sound recordings and performers ('Needletime rights') and defined collecting societies; Collecting Societies Regulations (2006) oversee establishment and operation of collecting societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Needletime royalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalties paid to artists and record companies for the copyright license to play sound recordings in public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting societies (e.g., SAMPRA, IMPRA) administer licensing and royalty collection for public performance and broadcast uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Needletime collecting societies (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two approved collecting societies in South Africa regulated by the CIPC Copyright Tribunal that collect Needletime royalties: SAMPRA and IMPRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SAMPRA administers Needletime rights for record labels and recording artists; IMPRA is an artists' royalty collecting society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry associations and collective management organisations
rubrics_metrics.description: Various associations and membership-based collection societies promote/protect copyright and manage royalties on behalf of members (e.g., PASA, MPASA, WGSA, RISA, SAMRO, DALRO, CAPASSO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These organisations handle licensing, administration and distribution of royalties, and provide sectoral support, networking and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and scope of registered designs
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered design protects the look or appearance of an article, not the underlying concept or idea (which is protected by patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration gives a limited-duration monopoly enforceable to prevent third parties from making the design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of design: aesthetic vs functional
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic design: protects visual features judged solely by the eye (shape, ornamentation, configuration, pattern). Functional design: protects features necessitated by the function of the article (pattern, shape, configuration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unique perfume bottle shape (aesthetic) – protected for 15 years; nozzle used to dispense liquid (functional) – protected for 10 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of novelty for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetic design must be new and original (look different from existing articles); a functional design must be new and not commonplace in the art (look different and not be obvious in the industry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design applications are examined only for formal compliance (no novelty assessment) — conduct searches before filing to assess novelty and uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production requirement for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: The article must be made by an industrial process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handcrafted items and works of art are generally excluded from registered design protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design release date / grace period
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for a registered design must be filed within six months of public disclosure; this 'grace period' cannot be extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep design confidential and do not market or sell the product until a design application has been filed. Public disclosure before filing may exclude foreign filing options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spare parts exclusion for functional designs
rubrics_metrics.description: A functional design cannot be filed for a spare part of a machine, vehicle, or equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider this limitation when seeking design protection for components or replacement parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of designs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Designs Register is divided into 32 classes and a registered design provides protection only in the class it is registered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same design may be filed in more than one class; South Africa follows the Locarno (Lacarno) classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design specification components
rubrics_metrics.description: A design application primarily includes: a set of representations illustrating the article; a 'Definitive Statement' setting out features for which protection is claimed; an 'Explanatory Statement' (optional except for IC layouts); and a 'Brief Statement of Features' published with a representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare clear representations and statements to define scope of protection; explanatory statement optional except where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representations requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Representations (commonly drawings but may be photographs) must properly depict the features of the design as applied to the article being protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure representations accurately show the design features to avoid ambiguity in the claimed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership/proprietor of a design application
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must be filed by the owner (proprietor): either the author, a person who caused the work to be created, an employer (work created in course and scope of employment), or a person to whom ownership has passed by assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure entitlement is clear and, where applicable, assignment or employment documentation supports the applicant's title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal examination only (designs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design applications are examined only for compliance with formal requirements and there is no assessment as to novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is recommended to conduct a search (basic or advanced) through the Register to assess novelty and uniqueness before filing; advanced searches carry additional cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design registration process steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing application (can be filed electronically); formal examination (acceptance/official action to comply with formal requirements); registration (certificate of grant issued); publication (notice of acceptance issued & advertise design); renewal (first renewal 3 years from release date and annually thereafter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow each administrative step and calendar renewals to maintain rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design renewal rules and lapse
rubrics_metrics.description: Registered designs must be renewed annually starting at the expiry of the third year calculated from the earlier of the date of lodgement, a priority date or a release date. The design will lapse if a renewal fee is not paid within a six month extension period after the renewal due date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor renewal schedule carefully to avoid lapse; use extension period if needed but risks lapse if not paid within extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of protection for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetic design has a duration of 15 years, and a functional design has a duration of 10 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terms of protection cannot be extended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign design filings (Paris Convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa is a member of the Paris Convention, which allows an applicant of a South African design to file foreign design applications in a country or region within six months of the local filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan disclosure and international filing strategy to preserve foreign filing rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent law scope and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents in South Africa are governed by the Patents Act, 57 of 1978 and accompanying Patent Regulations which provide details of patentable requirements, excluded subject matter, application and grant process, renewals and duration, infringement and invalidity, and enforcement/revocation mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the statute and regulations to guide filings and enforcement; consider counsel for litigation/enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention requirements (patentability criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be new/novel (not previously disclosed anywhere in the world), involve an inventive step (not obvious compared to existing products, knowledge and technology), and be useful or applicable in trade, industry, or agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct prior art searches for absolute novelty; keep invention confidential until filing; seek the services of a patent attorney for assessment and drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty guidance (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is absolute: disclosure anywhere in the world destroys novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct prior art searches (patents and publications, local and international). Maintain confidentiality prior to filing to preserve novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step requires that the invention is not obvious to a person in the field or industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess differences over prior art and whether those differences would have been obvious to a skilled practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility/usefulness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must have a practical application in the field or industry (useful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate applicability in trade, industry or agriculture where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject matter for patents
rubrics_metrics.description: What cannot be patented: a discovery; a scientific theory; a mathematical method; a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work; a scheme, rule, or method for performing a mental act, playing a game, or doing business; a programme for a computer; or the presentation of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Section 25 of the Patents Act for the statutory definitions and scope of exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor and ownership formalities (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'inventor' is the person(s) who came up with an invention and must always be listed when filing a patent application. The applicant (owner) of the patent must also be identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owner can be inventor or assignee; rights can be acquired by agreement or deed of assignment. Ensure all inventors are named and appropriate entitlement documents are submitted — misrepresentation may lead to revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent specification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent specification is a technical and legal document drafted to protect an invention and is normally accompanied by drawings which help to explain the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete specification must describe the invention in detail and set out claims defining the scope of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage patent filing procedure: provisional and complete
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial provisional patent application can be filed to obtain an official number with a filing date; followed by a complete patent application required to obtain granted rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional: individuals may draft/file their own; must fairly describe the invention; provides 12 months to develop or market; not open to public inspection. Complete: must be filed within 12 months of provisional; must be drafted and filed by a patent attorney; includes claims to define protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for completing patent filings (local, PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete patent application options include a South African complete patent application (local filing) or a PCT international patent application administered by WIPO covering many contracting states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT filing provides additional time (18 months) before separate national/regional filings are required; plan international strategy and deadlines accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patent filings and Paris Convention priority
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete patent application can be filed directly into a foreign jurisdiction by claiming priority under the Paris Convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Paris priority to secure filing dates in foreign jurisdictions; be mindful of national requirements and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation: patent covers what is disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application can only cover that which is disclosed in the accompanying specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If developments or modifications go beyond the initial disclosure, a second filing will be necessary to include those changes in the subject matter claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent renewal fees and lapse
rubrics_metrics.description: To maintain a patent, annual renewal fees are payable from the third anniversary of the filing date. The patent will lapse if a renewal fee is not paid within a six-month extension period after the renewal due date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track renewal schedules and use allowable extensions carefully to avoid unintended lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of protection for patents
rubrics_metrics.description: South African patents have a duration of 20 years, which cannot be extended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan commercialization and enforcement strategies within the statutory term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding patent infringement (practical guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid infringing an existing patent: check patent databases for relevant patents; review the claims; and modify your product accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your product cannot use the same combination of features covered by the claims of an existing patent. Adding features will not prevent infringement; to avoid infringement you must leave out one or more features of the patent claim. A patent attorney can assist with searching and advice.
